extracted.intended_audience: graduate and advanced undergraduate students of algebraic geometry (Math 216 course)
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions, properties, and constructions concerning the pullback of (quasi)coherent sheaves on schemes (including several equivalent constructions and their consequences), together with the description of morphisms to projective space via line bundles and sections, gluing along closed subschemes, and an extension theorem for curves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affine-local description of pullback
rubrics_metrics.description: On affines: if Spec A ⊂ X maps to Spec B ⊂ Y and G|Spec B corresponds to a B-module N, then Γ(Spec A, π^*G) should be identified with N ⊗_B A (canonical isomorphism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This affine-local tensor-product description motivates the definition and is the basis for gluing constructions; it is the starting point for proving properties. One may either use this to construct π^*G by gluing or show any other construction admits the natural identification (see §16.3.2–16.3.3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal property (adjointness) definition of pullback
rubrics_metrics.description: Define π^*G as an O_X-module characterized (up to unique isomorphism) by the adjointness: for any O_X-module F there are functorial bijections Hom_OX(π^*G, F) ≅ Hom_OY(G, π_*F).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This universal-property viewpoint is elegant and determines π^*G uniquely; it is local on the target (restriction compatibility). It requires existence of the representing object (hence constructions must be shown to satisfy it). Works naturally in category of O-modules, avoiding immediate quasicoherence questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit ringed-space construction of pullback
rubrics_metrics.description: As O_X-module: π^*G := π^{-1}G ⊗_{π^{-1}O_Y} O_X (use inverse image of sheaves and the structure morphism π^{-1}O_Y → O_X).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This short construction works for ringed spaces in general and can be shown to satisfy the universal property (hence coincides with affine-local construction and yields existence of pullback as a functor Mod_OY → Mod_OX).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pullback preserves the structure sheaf
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a canonical isomorphism π^*O_Y ≅ O_X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immediate from the definition; used repeatedly (e.g., to pull back sections identified as maps O_Y → G).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation of finite type and coherence
rubrics_metrics.description: If G is a finite type quasicoherent sheaf on Y then π^*G is finite type on X; hence if X is locally Noetherian and G is coherent then π^*G is coherent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caveat: pullback does not always preserve coherence in general (exercise suggests counterexamples). Use the locally Noetherian hypothesis when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pullback of vector bundles and transition functions
rubrics_metrics.description: If G is locally free of rank r on Y, then π^*G is locally free of rank r on X; moreover, trivializing neighborhoods {U_i} pull back to {π^{-1}U_i} and transition matrices pull back: π^*(T_{ij}) are transition matrices for π^*G.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In particular invertible sheaves pull back to invertible sheaves. This description is useful to understand pullback on concrete bundles via transition functions (Theorem 16.3.7(3)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Functoriality in the morphism
rubrics_metrics.description: For composable morphisms ξ: W → X and π: X → Y there is a canonical isomorphism ξ^* π^* G ≅ (π ∘ ξ)^* G.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This expresses that pullback is functorial in maps of schemes; the isomorphism is canonical and used often when changing base.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functoriality in the sheaf (π^* is a functor)
rubrics_metrics.description: π^* defines a functor QCoh(Y) → QCoh(X) (under hypotheses ensuring quasicoherence is preserved).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One must check hypotheses (quasicompact, quasiseparated) to ensure π^* sends QCoh to QCoh; but as a construction on O-modules it is always functorial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pullback of sections and vanishing loci
rubrics_metrics.description: A section s of G (a map O_Y → G) pulls back to a section π^*s: O_X → π^*G; the pullback of the locus where s vanishes is the locus where π^*s vanishes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine with π^*O_Y ≅ O_X and stalk/fiber formulas to reason about zeros of pulled-back sections; useful when pulling back divisors/hyperplanes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stalk formula for pullback
rubrics_metrics.description: If π(p)=q then (π^*G)_p ≅ G_q ⊗_{O_{Y,q}} O_{X,p}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives a local (germ-level) description of the pulled-back sheaf; used to deduce fiber and other local properties (Theorem 16.3.7(7)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fiber formula for pullback
rubrics_metrics.description: On fibers: (π^*G)|_p ≅ G|_q ⊗_{κ(q)} κ(p) when π(p)=q (i.e., pulled-back fibers are base-changed by residue field extension).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow from stalk formula by tensoring with residue fields; used to compute ranks and fibers of vector bundles after pullback (Theorem 16.3.7(8)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compatibility with tensor product
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The pullback commutes with tensor products of quasicoherent sheaves (Theorem 16.3.7(9)); prove using affine-local tensor product behavior and localization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right-exactness of pullback
rubrics_metrics.description: Pullback is a right-exact functor (but not left-exact in general).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This follows from the right-exactness of tensor product; an explicit counterexample shows pullback need not be left-exact (see Exercise 16.3.F). Useful to check exactness hypotheses or invoke flatness to get full exactness.

rubrics_metrics.name: When pullback sends QCoh to QCoh (quasicompact/quasiseparated hypothesis)
rubrics_metrics.description: If π: X → Y is quasicompact and quasiseparated then π^* sends QCoh_Y to QCoh_X and π^* and π_* are an adjoint pair between QCoh categories (Proposition 16.3.6).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The quasicompact & quasiseparated hypotheses are there solely to ensure quasicoherence is preserved; see Theorem 13.3.F for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flatness characterized by exactness of pullback
rubrics_metrics.description: A morphism π is flat if and only if the functor π^* from quasicoherent sheaves on Y to quasicoherent sheaves on X is exact (not merely right-exact).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives an important operational notion of flatness; the text returns to a different equivalent definition later (Chapter 24).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pullback of ideal sheaves: image vs. equality and flatness caveat
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a closed embedding i: X ↪ Y and a base-change µ: Y' → Y, the natural map µ^*(I_{X/Y}) → I_{X'/Y'} need not be an isomorphism in general; µ^*(I_{X/Y}) maps onto I_{X'/Y'} but equality may fail. If µ is flat then µ^*(I_{X/Y}) ≅ I_{X'/Y'}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This phenomenon stems from right-exactness of µ^*; afﬁne-locally the ideal of the pullback is generated by pullbacks of generators, but kernels need not pull back. Exercise 16.3.F gives an explicit counterexample.

rubrics_metrics.name: Push-pull (base-change) and projection formulas exist (natural morphisms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a commutative diagram (base-change square), there are natural morphisms relating ψ^* π_* and π'_* (ψ'^*), and there is a projection-formula morphism (π_*F) ⊗ G → π_*(F ⊗ π^*G).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In special situations (e.g., fiber squares, hypotheses on morphisms, or G locally free) these natural morphisms become isomorphisms (see Exercises 16.3.G and 16.3.H). Helpful hints: first handle the fiber diagram case and the case where G is free.

rubrics_metrics.name: Morphisms to projective space via invertible sheaf + sections (Theorem 16.4.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: For fixed scheme X, morphisms X → P^n are in bijection with data (L, s_0, ..., s_n) where L is an invertible sheaf and s_i are global sections of L with no common zeroes, up to isomorphism of these data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives a coordinate-free description of maps to projective space: given sections with no common zeros one builds the map, and conversely pullback of OP^n(1) and its standard hyperplane sections recover (L, s_i). Keep L and its sections in mind whenever you see a map to P^n. See Exercise 16.4.J for a functorial/coordinate-free version.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for closed embedding from linear series
rubrics_metrics.description: Given (L, s_0, ..., s_n) with associated morphism π: X → P^n, π is a closed embedding iff (i) each open set X_{s_i} is affine, and (ii) for each i the map of rings A[y_0,...,y_n] → Γ(X_{s_i}, O) sending y_j ↦ s_j / s_i is surjective (Exercise 16.4.D).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a concrete way to check when the linear series yields an embedding: affineness of the standard patches plus surjectivity onto coordinate rings. Use it to check Veronese/Segre embeddings and other examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Base-point-free linear series produce morphisms; nondegeneracy criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: A finite-dimensional base-point-free linear series V ⊂ Γ(X, L) induces a morphism φ_V: X → P(V^∨). The series (or X) is nondegenerate iff V → Γ(X, L) is injective (equivalently the image is not contained in a hyperplane).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complete linear series are base-point-free and thus nondegenerate; use these criteria to recognize images like rational normal curves (Examples 16.4.5–16.4.6 and Exercises 16.4.E–16.4.F).

rubrics_metrics.name: Affine model for gluing along closed subschemes (motivating example)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X_i = Spec A_i and Z_i = Spec A_i / I_i with an isomorphism φ: A_2/I_2 ≅ A_1/I_1, then the glued scheme is Spec R where R := A_1 ×_{A_1/I_1 ≅ A_2/I_2} A_2 (the fibered product of rings of pairs that agree modulo the ideals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This affine-fibered-product model motivates the general locally-ringed-space construction and is used to check local properties when gluing two schemes along isomorphic closed subschemes (see 16.4.12 and Exercises 16.4.L–N).

rubrics_metrics.name: Gluing two schemes along isomorphic closed subschemes (general construction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given closed embeddings Z_i ↪ X_i and an isomorphism φ: Z_1 ≅ Z_2, one can glue X_1 and X_2 along φ to produce a locally ringed space X_1 ⊔_φ X_2; the structure sheaf is defined by compatible germs that agree on the overlap (Exercises 16.4.L–16.4.N).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define topology by making opens those whose restrictions are open in both pieces; define stalks as pairs of compatible germs agreeing via φ on Z. Check that away from the glued locus the result is a scheme and locally model it on the affine example to show the glued space is a scheme in neighborhoods (Exercise 16.4.M).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation of properties under gluing (proper, separated, finite type)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X_1 and X_2 satisfy properties like being universally closed (proper), separated, or finite type over a Noetherian ring A, then the glued scheme X_1 ⊔_φ X_2 also has these properties (Exercise 16.4.O).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof reduces to the affine motivating example and uses finiteness arguments (Noetherianness) and generators of ideals to show the corresponding ring R has the required finiteness/closedness/separatedness properties; in particular properness is preserved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curve-to-projective extension criterion (Theorem 16.5.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let C be a pure-dimension-1 Noetherian scheme over an affine base S, and p a regular closed point of C. If Y is a projective S-scheme then any morphism C \ {p} → Y (of S-schemes) extends uniquely to all of C.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice S = Spec k and C a k-curve; the extension is unique (reduced-to-separated theorem/Cartier divisor arguments). Exercises (16.5.A) give counterexamples showing hypotheses are necessary (projectivity of Y, 1-dimensionality and nonsingularity of C cannot be dropped). The result connects concrete geometry of curves to projectivity and properness considerations.
